paras: The beating of a hotel porter in Hinton, West Virginia, was an assault on a Black porter by a man named Farris on the morning of 25 December 1881. Farris was arrested and brought before the mayor, but his friends' anger at the arresting officer led to an armed attack on the town's police the next night. Only the Richmond Dispatch's Hinton correspondent reported the beating; other papers carried only the attack on the police.

On Christmas morning, a Sunday, three men described as 'drunken rowdies' were walking down Third street when they passed a Black man. One of them, Farris, 'commenced to beat most unmercifully and without the least provocation' the man, who fled into the Central Hotel, where he worked as porter. The hotel's proprietor reported the assault to Mayor Benedict, who sent policeman John Palmer to arrest Farris.

Farris resisted but was brought to the mayor's office, and some of his friends followed with the aim of taking him from the officers. The rescue failed, but pistols were 'freely drawn' during the hearing, though no shots were fired. Farris was then allowed to leave; a garble in the printed text leaves unclear whether he was fined or simply let go.

Palmer, a newcomer to the force, was disliked by Farris and his friends, who threatened to mob him. On Monday night Palmer and Policeman Fred McCreery were attacked on Summers street; the Dispatch put the attackers at fifteen or twenty, while the Hinton Herald counted ten or twelve. McCreery was shot near the knee and beaten, and Palmer escaped into the mayor's office under fire.

A deputy sheriff summoned a posse, but the men fled, and warrants were issued for Beardon, Michaels and Faris as the ringleaders, who were said to have left the state. No further action on the beating of the porter appears in the coverage.

The Dispatch letter, headed 'Too Much Christmas—A Row', presented the porter's beating as the start of a drunken holiday disturbance and called the later attack on the police a 'cowardly act'. The Staunton Spectator, quoting the Hinton Herald, called the Monday attack 'a serious affray', the West Virginia Freeman listed it among Christmas whisky crimes as a 'disgraceful fracas', and the Staunton Vindicator gave it one sentence. None of these later items mentioned the porter or his race.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch Hinton correspondent
accounts.gist: Farris beat a Black porter without provocation, was arrested and heard by the mayor while his friends tried to rescue him, and was let go; on Monday night a mob of fifteen or twenty attacked the two policemen.

accounts.label: Hinton Herald (via Staunton Spectator)
accounts.gist: Ten or twelve men assaulted the sergeant and special policeman McCreery about 7 o'clock Monday night; warrants were issued for Beardon, Michaels and Faris. The porter is not mentioned.

framing.detail: The Dispatch headline 'Too Much Christmas—A Row' treats the porter's beating as the opening of a drunken row, calls it unprovoked, and gives most space to the attack on the police as a 'cowardly act'.
The Staunton and Parkersburg papers carried only the attack on the police, as 'a serious affray', a 'disgraceful fracas' and 'disorder nearly amounting to a riot'.
